items.correctExplanation: Right — Earth spins eastward, so the sun appears to travel west. Sunrises are Earth's doing, not the sun's.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — eastward spin. Earth rotates toward the east, carrying us into the sunlight each dawn.
items.lessonContent:
Apparent sky motion usually means Earth moved, not the sky.
Rotation explains days; orbit explains years.
Ask 'who moved?' before trusting your eyes.
Share this: watch one sunset as Earth's turning.
items.question: Why does the sun rise in the east every morning?
items.title: The Eastern Dawn

items.correctExplanation: Correct — phases show how much of the sunlit half faces us. The moon's own geometry, not shadows, writes the calendar.
items.incorrectExplanation: Actually, sunlit angles. We see changing slices of the moon's lit half as it orbits.
items.lessonContent:
Phases are geometry lessons written in light.
Half the moon always shines; angles hide the rest.
Orbit positions predict phases precisely.
Share this: predict tonight's phase from last week's.
items.question: What causes the moon's changing phases?
items.title: The Monthly Face

items.correctExplanation: Yes — the tilted axis aims hemispheres toward or away from the sun. Tilt, not distance, deals summer and winter.
items.incorrectExplanation: Close! Axial tilt. Earth's lean aims each hemisphere sunward in turn; distance barely matters.
items.lessonContent:
Tilt beats distance in the seasons contest.
Closest approach happens in January's cold.
Angles of sunlight set the thermal year.
Share this: explain summer with a tilted ball and lamp.
items.question: What causes Earth's seasons?
items.title: The Tilted Year

items.correctExplanation: Right — the moon's pull plus Earth's spin raise two daily bulges. Tides are the moon's signature on oceans.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — lunar gravity. The moon hauls water into bulges; coastlines rotate through them twice daily.
items.lessonContent:
Tides are gravity made visible twice daily.
The moon leads; the sun merely assists.
Spinning Earth ferries coasts through bulges.
Share this: check tide times against moonrise once.
items.question: What mainly raises the ocean tides?
items.title: The Twice-Daily Sea

items.correctExplanation: Correct — the moon rotates once per orbit, tidally locked. We always face the same half.
items.incorrectExplanation: Actually, synchronous spin. The moon turns exactly as fast as it circles, hiding its far side forever.
items.lessonContent:
Tidal locking synchronizes spins with orbits.
Gravity's grip slows moons into lockstep.
Many moons show one face eternally.
Share this: spin once per lap around a chair.
items.question: Why do we always see the same face of the moon?
items.title: The Loyal Face

items.correctExplanation: Yes — Earth needs 365¼ days per orbit, and leap days collect the quarters. Calendars drift without them.
items.incorrectExplanation: Close! Quarter-day surplus. Each orbit overshoots 365 days by six hours; February banks them.
items.lessonContent:
Orbits ignore round numbers — calendars compensate.
Leftover fractions accumulate into whole days.
Precision timekeeping banks the remainders.
Share this: explain February 29th with fractions.
items.question: Why do leap years exist?
items.title: The Extra Day

items.correctExplanation: Right — faster inner Earth laps slower Mars, which seems to reverse. Retrograde is a passing-lane illusion.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — Earth overtakes it. Our faster orbit laps Mars, making it appear to backtrack.
items.lessonContent:
Overtaking creates backward illusions everywhere.
Faster lanes lap slower traffic apparently backward.
Reference frames fool drivers and astronomers.
Share this: watch cars 'reverse' from a fast train.
items.question: Why does Mars sometimes appear to move backward?
items.title: The Backward Wanderer

items.correctExplanation: Correct — only during lunar eclipses does Earth's shadow touch the moon. Eclipses are alignments, phases are angles.
items.incorrectExplanation: Actually, Earth blocks sunlight. Perfect sun-Earth-moon lineups drape the moon in copper shadow.
items.lessonContent:
Eclipses need three-body straight lines.
Shadows enter only at perfect alignment.
Copper moons betray bent sunlight.
Share this: catch the next eclipse's copper hue.
items.question: What darkens the moon during a lunar eclipse?
items.title: The Copper Moon

items.correctExplanation: Yes — Mars wears oxidized iron like old tools. Rust, planet-wide, paints the red planet.
items.incorrectExplanation: Close! Rusted iron dust. Iron in Martian soil oxidized over eons into global rust.
items.lessonContent:
Chemistry paints planets from palettes of elements.
Oxidation reddens iron wherever air or water was.
Colors diagnose compositions remotely.
Share this: name one earthly rust spot matching Mars.
items.question: Why does Mars look red?
items.title: The Rusty Planet

items.correctExplanation: Right — countless ice and rock chunks circle Saturn's equator. Rings are debris in disciplined formation.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — orbiting ice rubble. Tides shredded a moon into glittering lanes.
items.lessonContent:
Rings are moons that wandered too close.
Gravity sculpts debris into flat lanes.
Ice gleams brightest in ring systems.
Share this: spot Saturn's rings in binoculars.
items.question: What are Saturn's rings made of?
items.title: The Icy Halo

items.correctExplanation: Correct — Venus's CO2 shroud traps heat relentlessly. Blankets beat proximity in the temperature contest.
items.incorrectExplanation: Actually, trapping blanket gas. Carbon dioxide smothers Venus hotter than closer Mercury.
items.lessonContent:
Atmospheres outrank orbits in heating planets.
Greenhouse gases blanket worlds remorselessly.
Venus warns what blankets can do.
Share this: feel a car greenhouse on a mild day.
items.question: Why is Venus hotter than Mercury despite being farther from the sun?
items.title: The Hottest Neighbor

items.correctExplanation: Yes — airless Mercury keeps no heat past sunset. Blankets, not distance, moderate climates.
items.incorrectExplanation: Close! No insulating air. Days roast and nights freeze where no atmosphere banks warmth.
items.lessonContent:
Air banks daytime heat for nighttime spending.
Airless worlds swing between extremes daily.
Blankets stabilize every climate they cover.
Share this: compare desert and coastal night chills.
items.question: Why does Mercury swing from scorching days to freezing nights?
items.title: The Swinging Thermometer

items.correctExplanation: Right — charged solar streams shove comet gas outward. Tails always flee the sun, head or tail first.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — solar wind streams. Sunlight pressure plus particles sweep tails anti-sunward.
items.lessonContent:
Solar wind sculpts every comet's streaming hair.
Tails point away regardless of travel direction.
Backward-flying tails betray the wind.
Share this: watch a comet's tail defy its motion.
items.question: Why do comet tails always point away from the sun?
items.title: The Fleeing Tail

items.correctExplanation: Correct — leftover building rubble circles between Mars and Jupiter. A planet that never quite assembled.
items.incorrectExplanation: Actually, Mars-Jupiter debris. Jupiter's gravity stirred the zone too violently for assembly.
items.lessonContent:
Failed planets litter the solar system's gaps.
Giant neighbors stir construction zones violently.
Debris belts fossilize formation history.
Share this: place the belt between Mars and Jupiter.
items.question: Where does the asteroid belt circle, and what is it?
items.title: The Unbuilt Planet

items.correctExplanation: Yes — stars are points that shimmer whole; planets are tiny disks averaging the wobble. Size steadies light.
items.incorrectExplanation: Close! Disks beat points. Planetary disks average atmospheric dancing that tosses star-points around.
items.lessonContent:
Twinkling diagnoses air, never stars themselves.
Disks average; points flicker fully.
Space telescopes escape the shimmer entirely.
Share this: compare one star and planet tonight.
items.question: Why do stars twinkle more than planets?
items.title: The Steady Wanderer

items.correctExplanation: Right — the sun blazes white; our air yellows it. Astronauts meet a white star.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — truly white-hot. Atmosphere scatters blue away, tinting noon gold.
items.lessonContent:
Air tints everything viewed through miles of it.
Sunsets redden through longer air paths.
True colors need vacuum vantage points.
Share this: note the sun whitens at noon.
items.question: What color is the sun really?
items.title: The White Star

items.correctExplanation: Correct — no wind or water smooths the moon. Footprints and craters outlive civilizations there.
items.incorrectExplanation: Actually, no erasing weather. Airless stillness preserves every scar for eons.
items.lessonContent:
Erosion needs movers: wind, water, life.
Still worlds remember every impact forever.
Earth's bustle buries its own history.
Share this: compare fresh and ancient craters online.
items.question: Why do moon craters survive billions of years?
items.title: The Scarred Face

items.correctExplanation: Yes — sound rides air molecules, and space offers none. Explosions bloom silently there.
items.incorrectExplanation: Close! No carrying air. Without molecules to compress, even blasts make no sound.
items.lessonContent:
Sound needs a medium to travel through.
Vacuum silences the mightiest blasts.
Movies lie loudly about space battles.
Share this: mute one film explosion knowingly.
items.question: Why is space completely silent?
items.title: The Silent Blast

items.correctExplanation: Right — the moon's smaller mass pulls gentler. Weight follows local gravity, mass stays yours.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — one-sixth gravity. Lunar pull is a sixth of Earth's, so scales read lighter.
items.lessonContent:
Weight is local; mass travels with you.
Scales read gravity's handshake, not your substance.
Every world weighs you differently.
Share this: compute your lunar weight tonight.
items.question: Why do astronauts weigh less on the moon?
items.title: The Lighter Step

items.correctExplanation: Correct — solar particles slide down magnetic field lines at the poles. Auroras are space weather made visible.
items.incorrectExplanation: Actually, polar particle rain. Charged sun-stuff strikes polar air, which glows in reply.
items.lessonContent:
Magnetic fields funnel solar storms poleward.
Glowing air reports invisible bombardment.
Space weather paints polar skies.
Share this: check aurora forecasts after solar news.
items.question: What paints the aurora across polar skies?
items.title: The Polar Fire

items.correctExplanation: Yes — the zone where water stays liquid, neither steam nor ice. Life's solvent sets the address.
items.incorrectExplanation: Close! Liquid-water orbit. Too close boils oceans; too far freezes them.
items.lessonContent:
Liquid water defines life's favorite neighborhood.
Solvents matter more than scenery for biology.
Zones shift with stellar brightness.
Share this: place Earth inside the sun's zone.
items.question: What defines the habitable Goldilocks zone?
items.title: The Just-Right Ring

items.correctExplanation: Right — Pluto shares its lane with Kuiper crowds. Planets gravitationally own their orbits; dwarfs rent.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — uncleared neighborhood. Pluto never swept its orbital zone clean.
items.lessonContent:
Planethood demands orbital dominance, not just roundness.
Clearing neighborhoods takes gravitational muscle.
Dwarfs share lanes; planets own them.
Share this: defend Pluto's dwarf status kindly.
items.question: Why was Pluto reclassified as a dwarf planet?
items.title: The Demoted World

items.correctExplanation: Correct — as Earth orbits, midnight faces different star fields. Our traveling window tours the galaxy yearly.
items.incorrectExplanation: Actually, night-side windows. The dark side aims at new constellations each season.
items.lessonContent:
Orbits tour stargazers through yearly galleries.
Midnight windows open on rotating exhibits.
Seasons change scenery above too.
Share this: greet one seasonal constellation's return.
items.question: Why do different constellations appear in different seasons?
items.title: The Turning Gallery

items.correctExplanation: Yes — Earth annually plows through old comet debris. Showers are calendar appointments with dust.
items.incorrectExplanation: Close! Comet-trail crossings. Each August Earth re-enters the same dusty stream.
items.lessonContent:
Debris streams mark comets' ancient highways.
Annual showers repeat like clockwork appointments.
Dust grains ignite as shooting stars.
Share this: watch one annual shower's peak night.
items.question: Why do meteor showers return on schedule yearly?
items.title: The Annual Rain

items.correctExplanation: Right — the horizon moon looks huge but measures identical. Brains inflate objects near landmarks.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — brain-size illusion. Photograph it: pixels prove the moon never grows.
items.lessonContent:
Brains scale objects against nearby landmarks.
Horizon frames inflate; zenith empties shrink.
Cameras expose perceptual inflations.
Share this: photograph the 'huge' moon tonight.
items.question: Why does the moon look giant near the horizon?
items.title: The Huge Moon
